transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-10-04
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Ellis (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO, Cobalt), Liam O'Connor (SRE Lead), Sophie Tan (Platform)

Summary:
Brief postmortem style technical deep dive to identify root cause of recurring p99 spikes observed on Cobalt's staging environment when traffic goes through their on-prem edge-proxy / VPC NAT during burst windows. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming behaviors, KV cache shard hotness, quantization kernel fallbacks, and multi-hop buffering at the proxy layer. Agree next steps to run joint load tests and exchange kernel traces.

Topics covered:
- Observed spikes and topological description (edge proxy -> VPC NAT -> Redwood private node)
- Streaming chunk vs non-streaming full response behavior
- KV cache prewarm and shard hotness leading to cold misses
- Quantized int8 kernel paths and occasional fallback to slower FP kernels
- TLS/reuse and proxy buffering/queueing behaviors
- Short term mitigations and longer term architecture changes

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. We wanted to keep this as a technical postmortem, walk through the traces you sent over, and then converge on a set of experiments. Daniel from our infra team is here to drive the kernel-level questions.
[00:18] Priya (Cobalt): Thanks Maya. We saw a couple of p99 jumps last Thursday during the 18:00 deploy smoke test. Nothing else changed on app level but latency shot up from ~120ms p95 to 600-900ms p99 for about 10 minutes.
[00:32] Daniel (Redwood SE): Ok, can you remind us of the exact network path for the staging calls? You have an on-prem edge proxy that does TLS terminate, then NAT into your VPC, then a private peering into Redwood dedicated pool, is that right?
[00:45] Sophie (Cobalt): Correct. Edge proxy (Envoy) terminates TLS and then does a mTLS to our VPC egress gateway which performs source nat, and then a straight route to Redwood private endpoints over the peering link.
[00:58] Liam (Cobalt SRE): One thing to flag, our proxy has a 16KB downstream buffer and we do per-connection keepalive reset every ~90s. We also run connection pooling but Envoy resets workers on deploys.
[01:11] Maya: Good detail. Two immediate suspect categories: network buffering / connection churn at the proxy and a server-side fallback in the model runtime (e.g., quant kernel fallback or cache miss cascade).
[01:25] Priya: We saw the p99s coincide with a short burst of small conversations from our QA harness—more short requests than usual. I'm wondering if streaming chunking vs full responses behavior changed.
[01:38] Daniel: That syncs with something we observed in a test: streaming emits many small frames, which interact poorly with proxies that buffer to 16KB before flushing. If the proxy waits, downstream grouping plus upstream batching can create awkward head-of-line waits.
[01:53] Sophie: So the streaming option could actually make tail worse if the proxy buffers? That seems counterintuitive.
[02:00] Daniel: Yeah, streaming is usually lower perceived latency for the user, but if an intermediate node buffers by bytes, streaming produces lots of small writes that sit in the buffer until threshold—so it creates batching at the network layer that wasn't intended.
[02:13] Liam: We also saw spikes align with a couple of internal KV shard rebalances last week; hotkeys shifted and a shard got cold then hot again. Possibly cache pressure when streaming emitted many small prefixes that didn't hit the KV cache.
[02:28] Maya: Ok so potential compound: proxy buffering + KV cold misses + runtime kernel fallback. Anyone have trace logs showing model runtime events?
[02:38] Priya: We uploaded logs, noted that at the times of spikes there were occasional "kernel fallback" warnings in Redwood's agent trace - something like quant_dequant falling back to slower path.
[02:50] Daniel: Right that's the important bit. In int8 paths some kernels are covered by optimized fused ops; if memory alignment or sequence length, or unexpected token shapes occur, the runtime can pick a conservative fallback kernel that is significantly slower. That combined with a cold KV miss can push you over.
[03:07] Sophie: Do we know why the fallback triggered only during the bursts?
[03:12] Daniel: Hypothesis: the QA harness churn created many short prefix-only requests that result in varied sequence lengths and more frequent branch in kernel selection code. Also if streaming splits messages differently, internal packing might produce shapes the fast kernel doesn't support, so it uses the slower generic kernel.
[03:27] Liam: We also noticed an increase in TCP connection resets in the same window; Envoy was recycling workers due to config reloads triggered by our deploys. That would break keepalive and force new TLS handshakes. TLS renegotiation plus kernel fallback plus cache miss is a bad combo.
[03:44] Maya: So we have a three-way: proxy buffering + TLS churn + slow kernel fallback + KV pressure. Any priority order thoughts?
[03:52] Daniel: If I had to rank immediate impact: kernel fallback + cache miss is server-heavy and likely largest single contributor. Proxy buffering and TLS churn amplify tail by adding tens to hundreds of ms per request.
[04:05] Priya: How do we verify the kernel fallback hypothesis?
[04:08] Daniel: We need the per-request runtime decision traces showing kernel selection, and a micro-benchmark that forces the same sequence length/shape and streaming chunking pattern. Redwood can run a targeted load that mimics the QA harness streaming pattern through the exact same proxy topology.
[04:25] Maya: We'll do that. We'll also instrument Envoy with flow logs and dump proxy buffer stats.
[04:31] Sophie: Could quantization itself be the issue? We use int8 to save cost. If the quantized model path is brittle, is fallback common?
[04:40] Daniel: In our experience, well-tested quant profiles rarely fallback in steady-state, but corner shapes do trigger it. Also some older kernels have alignment or instruction set dependencies; on certain CPU/GPU combos the runtime will choose the generic kernel which is slower. We want to check hardware telemetry too.
[04:55] Liam: Our staging uses a mixed fleet of older nVidia and newer GPUs; maybe the kernel packing behaves differently.
[05:02] Daniel: Exactly. Mixed fleet plus per-node kernel availability can create performance variance — hot path on new GPUs but fallback on older ones. That can show as long-tail.
[05:12] Priya: What about streaming vs non-streaming? Should we disable streaming while we debug?
[05:18] Maya: We typically suggest an experiment: run identical load with streaming enabled and disabled across the same topology and compare p95/p99 plus trace-level kernel decisions. Streaming might improve perceived latency for normal cases but worsen tail under buffering.
[05:32] Sophie: Ok, practical mitigations?
[05:35] Daniel: Short term: 1) Force runtime to prefer the quantized kernel (pin quant profile) where safe; 2) Prewarm KV cache for the hot prefixes your QA harness uses; 3) Increase Envoy flush window or disable buffering for these routes; 4) Increase connection reuse (keepalive) to reduce TLS handshakes during deploys.
[05:51] Liam: We can bump keepalive and look into not recycling workers mid-load. But disabling buffering at Envoy may have downstream throughput penalties.
[05:58] Maya: For a medium-term fix, consider zoning: have an edge L7 proxy that forwards streaming directly to Redwood via a persistent connection pool so fewer hops and less per-request reinit. Also you could route low-latency paths to dedicated nodes.
[06:12] Priya: Makes sense. Any data we should collect to help prioritize?
[06:15] Daniel: Per-request: kernel-select trace, KV hit/miss, per-hop latency (edge->vpc->redwood), TLS handshake indicator, and queuing time at Envoy. If you can correlate p99 spikes to kernel fallback events that proves the hypothesis.
[06:28] Sophie: We have partial telemetry; we'll export the envoy stats and the peering router logs.
[06:33] Maya: Great. We'll run a controlled load - Redwood will emulate the QA harness pattern including streaming small chunks and non-streaming full responses, through your staging proxy. We'll capture traces on both sides.
[06:45] Liam: Timeline — we can get Envoy dumps in 48 hours, and Priya will confirm a bench window next week.
[06:52] Maya: Sounds good. A couple more detailed questions from our side: how often do you see the hotkey churn and are key prefixes stable?
[07:00] Sophie: The hotkey churn was triggered by an internal migration, so ephemeral, but our QA traffic tends to use similar prefixes repeatedly for regressions.
[07:08] Daniel: Ok, then prewarm is feasible. Also for the kernel fallback, can you list the GPU SKUs in staging?
[07:14] Liam: We have a mix: some T4-ish older cards and newer A10s.
[07:18] Daniel: That explains per-node variance. Our runtime picks different kernels. We can also produce a quant build tuned for mixed fleet that avoids the problematic code path.
[07:26] Priya: Is there a risk of quality regression if you force a particular kernel?
[07:30] Daniel: We run functional evals by default when changing quant profiles. If you approve a short pilot, we can validate outputs on your prompt set.
[07:38] Maya: Ok let's summarize and assign owners.
[07:41] Maya: Redwood will run two load tests: 1) streaming pattern through your staging proxy topology; 2) non-streaming pattern. We'll capture kernel traces and per-hop latencies.
[07:52] Daniel: I'll run the kernel trace experiment and produce a short write-up of early indicators.
[07:57] Priya: We'll export envoy and router logs and confirm bench time.
[08:02] Liam: We'll also adjust keepalive and postpone worker restarts during bench windows.
[08:06] Sophie: And I'll work on the KV prewarm script to hit the hot prefixes before test.
[08:12] Maya: Cool. Final Qs?
[08:15] Priya: One ask: what's the cost delta for using dedicated nodes for these low-latency routes?
[08:20] Maya: I'll send a pilot pricing sheet. Dedicated tends to reduce variance because your traffic lands on a homogeneous fleet and we can guarantee kernel availability.
[08:29] Daniel: Also note that enabling streaming with a tuned proxy gives best perceived latency once the buffering config is resolved.
[08:36] Priya: Alright thanks, this was useful.
[08:40] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the test plan and timeline.

Recap / Key outcomes:
- Likely root cause is a combination of: quant kernel fallback (mixed GPU fleet) + KV cache misses + proxy buffering + TLS churn.
- Immediate experiments: controlled streaming vs non-streaming load across same topology; kernel-selection traces; proxy buffer tuning; KV prewarm.
- Short term mitigations: pin quant profile for pilot, increase keepalive, prewarm KV, avoid worker restarts during load windows.
